items.title: Step 1
items.description:
In this workshop, you will practice working with various string methods used for formatting strings.

Start by creating a variable called `userInput` and assign it the following value: `"   Hello World!   "`.

hints.text: You should have a `userInput` variable.
Your `userInput` variable should be a string.
You should assign `"   Hello World!   "` to your `userInput` variable. Make sure there are three spaces before the `H` and three spaces after the `!`.

items.title: Step 2
items.description: Next, add a `console.log()` with the string `"Original input:"`.

hints.text: You should log the string `"Original input:"` to the console.

items.beforeEach:
const spy = __helpers.spyOn(console, 'log');
const getLogs = () => spy.calls.map(call => call?.[0]);

items.title: Step 3
items.description: Below your first `console.log()`, add another `console.log()` to log the `userInput` variable to the console.

hints.text: You should log the `userInput` variable to the console.

items.seed:
const userInput = "   Hello World!   ";
console.log("Original input:");
items.beforeEach:
const spy = __helpers.spyOn(console, 'log');
const getLogs = () => spy.calls.map(call => call?.[0]);

items.title: Step 4
items.description:
Your `userInput` value has some extra spaces at both ends of the string. To create a new string with that whitespace removed, you can use the `trim()` method.  

Here is an example:

```js
const sentence = "  Learning about the trim method.  ";
sentence.trim(); // "Learning about the trim method."
```

Create a variable named `cleanedInput` and assign it the result of using the `trim()` method on the `userInput` variable.

hints.text: You should have a `cleanedInput` variable.
Your `cleanedInput` variable should be a string.
You should assign `userInput.trim()` to your `cleanedInput` variable.

items.title: Step 5
items.description:
Now it is time to see the result.

Start by adding a `console.log()` with the string `"Result of trimming whitespace from both ends:"`.

Then below that `console.log()`, add another `console.log()` with the `cleanedInput` variable.

hints.text: You should log the string `"Result of trimming whitespace from both ends:"` to the console.
hints.test: assert.equal(getLogs()[2], "Result of trimming whitespace from both ends:");

hints.text: You should log the `cleanedInput` variable to the console.

items.beforeEach:
const spy = __helpers.spyOn(console, 'log');
const getLogs = () => spy.calls.map(call => call?.[0]);

items.title: Step 6
items.description:
There will be times where you will want to only trim whitespace at the beginning of the string. That is where the `trimStart()` method comes in handy.

Here is an example:

```js
const sentence = "  I love learning.  ";
sentence.trimStart(); // "I love learning.  "
```

Remember that strings are immutable. This method will create a new string with the result. Not modify the original one.

Create a variable `trimmedStart` and assign it the result of using the `trimStart()` method on the `userInput` variable.

hints.text: You should have a `trimmedStart` variable.
Your `trimmedStart` variable should be a string.
You should assign `userInput.trimStart()` to your `trimmedStart` variable.

items.title: Step 7
items.description:
Now it is time to see the results of trimming whitespace at the beginning of the string.

Below your `trimmedStart` variable, add a `console.log()` with the string `"After using the trimStart() method, leading spaces removed:"`. 

Then below that `console.log()`, add another `console.log()` with the `trimmedStart` variable.

hints.text: You should log the string `"After using the trimStart() method, leading spaces removed:"` to the console.
hints.test: assert.equal(getLogs()[4], "After using the trimStart() method, leading spaces removed:");

hints.text: You should log the `trimmedStart` variable to the console.

items.title: Step 8
items.description:
To trim whitespace at the end of a string, you can use the `trimEnd()` method.

Here is an example:

```js
const sentence = "  I love learning.  ";
sentence.trimEnd(); // "  I love learning."
```

Create a variable called `trimmedEnd` and assign it the result of using the `trimEnd()` method on the `userInput` variable.

hints.text: You should have a `trimmedEnd` variable.
Your `trimmedEnd` variable should be a string.
You should assign `userInput.trimEnd()` to your `trimmedEnd` variable.

items.title: Step 9
items.description:
Now it is time to see the results of trimming whitespace at the end of the string.

Below your `trimmedEnd` variable, add a `console.log()` with the string `"After using the trimEnd() method, trailing spaces removed:"`. 

Then below that `console.log()`, add another `console.log()` with the `trimmedEnd` variable.

hints.text: You should log the string `"After using the trimEnd() method, trailing spaces removed:"` to the console.
hints.test: assert.equal(getLogs()[6], "After using the trimEnd() method, trailing spaces removed:");

hints.text: You should log the `trimmedEnd` variable to the console.

items.title: Step 10
items.description:
There will be times where you will need to create a new string with a different casing. 

To create a new string with all of the letters converted to uppercase, you can use the `toUpperCase()` method.

Here is an example:

```js
const sentence = "I love to code!";
sentence.toUpperCase(); // "I LOVE TO CODE!"
```

Create a variable called `upperCaseInput` and assign it the result of using the `toUpperCase()` method on the `cleanedInput` variable.

hints.text: You should have a `upperCaseInput` variable.
Your `upperCaseInput` variable should be a string.
You should assign `cleanedInput.toUpperCase()` to your `upperCaseInput` variable.

items.title: Step 11
items.description:
Now it is time to see the results.

Below your `upperCaseInput` variable, add a `console.log()` with the string `"Result of using the toUpperCase() method:"`. 

Then below that `console.log()`, add another `console.log()` with the `upperCaseInput` variable.

hints.text: You should log the string `"Result of using the toUpperCase() method:"` to the console.
hints.test: assert.equal(getLogs()[8], "Result of using the toUpperCase() method:");

hints.text: You should log the `upperCaseInput` variable to the console.

items.title: Step 12
items.description:
If you need to create a new string where all of the letters are in lowercase, you can use the `toLowerCase()` method.  

Start by creating a variable called `lowerCaseInput` and assign it the result of using the `toLowerCase()` method on the `cleanedInput` variable. 

Then log the string `"Result of using the toLowerCase() method:"`.

Finally, add another `console.log()` for the `lowerCaseInput` variable.

Your `lowerCaseInput` variable should be a string.
You should assign `cleanedInput.toLowerCase()` to your `lowerCaseInput` variable.
You should log the string `"Result of using the toLowerCase() method:"` to the console.
hints.test: assert.equal(getLogs()[10], "Result of using the toLowerCase() method:");

hints.text: You should log the `lowerCaseInput` variable to the console.

items.title: Step 13
items.description:
There will be times where you will need to use multiple methods to create a new string. Over the next few steps, you will use some of the methods you have learned so far to create a new string that uses the camelCase naming convention.

Start by creating a variable called `lowercaseWord` and assign it the string `"camelcase"`. 

Below that `lowercaseWord` variable, create another variable called `camelCasedVersion` and assign it an empty string for now.

Below that `camelCasedVersion` variable, add a `console.log()` with the string `"Camel cased version:"` followed by another `console.log()` for the `camelCasedVersion` variable.

hints.text: You should have a variable called `lowercaseWord`.
Your `lowercaseWord` should be a string.
You should assign the string `"camelcase"` to your `lowercaseWord` variable.
You should have a `camelCasedVersion` variable.
Your `camelCasedVersion` variable should be a string.
You should assign an empty string to your `camelCasedVersion` variable.
You should log the string `"Camel cased version:"` to the console.
You should log the `camelCasedVersion` variable to the console.

items.beforeEach:
const spy = __helpers.spyOn(console, 'log');
const getLogs = () => spy.calls.map(call => call?.[0]);

items.title: Step 14
items.description:
As you recall from earlier lessons and workshops, you can extract portions of a string by using the `slice()` method.

Here is a reminder:

```js
const str = "abcd";
str.slice(0, 3); // "abc"
```

You should change the existing `camelCasedVersion` assignment by replacing the empty string with `lowercaseWord.slice(0, 5)`.

Now you should see the word `"camel"` in the console.

hints.text: Your `camelCasedVersion` variable should not be an empty string.
You should assign `lowercaseWord.slice(0, 5)` to the `camelCasedVersion` variable.
You should NOT assign the literal string `"camel"` to the `camelCasedVersion`. Please reread through the instructions for the correct approach.

items.title: Step 15
items.description:
As you recall from earlier lessons, the camelCase naming convention starts with a lowercase letter for the first word, and each subsequent word begins with an uppercase letter followed by lowercase letters.

Here are some reminder examples: 

```md
freeCodeCamp
camelCase
learningIsFun
```

The second word in the `lowercaseWord` variable is `"case"`. To access the `c` in that word, you can use `lowercaseWord[5]`. 

Update the `camelCasedVersion` assignment to use the `+` operator to concatenate `lowercaseWord.slice(0, 5)` with the result of using the correct method for converting strings to uppercase on `lowercaseWord[5]`.

Now you should see `camelC` in the console.

hints.text: You should concatenate `lowercaseWord.slice(0, 5)` with `lowercaseWord[5].toUpperCase()`.
You should NOT assign the literal string `"camelC"` to the `camelCasedVersion`. Please re read through the instructions for the correct approach.

items.title: Step 16
items.description:
Right now your `camelCasedVersion` variable holds the value of `camelC`. But the desired result is `camelCase`. 

To get the remaining `ase` letters, you can use the `slice()` method with a negative index value. Recall, that using negative index values tells the `slice()` method to extract from the end. 

Here is a reminder example:

```js
const str = "abcd";
str.slice(-2); // cd
```

Update the `camelCasedVersion` assignment to also concatenate `lowercaseWord.slice(0, 5) + lowercaseWord[5].toUpperCase()` with the result of using the `slice()` method on `lowercaseWord`. Pass in the number `-3` for the `slice()` method.

And with that last change, your workshop is complete!

hints.text: You should concatenate `lowercaseWord.slice(0, 5) + lowercaseWord[5].toUpperCase()` with `lowercaseWord.slice(-3)`.
You should NOT assign the literal string `"camelCase"` to the `camelCasedVersion`. Please re read through the instructions for the correct approach.
